lawyer:
SR Pal, Sr. Advocate, with BN Chowdhury, Advocate, instructed by A Rub II, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellants.
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Advocate instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondents 1-4.
parties:
Sudhangshu Kumar Chowdhury and another ----- Appellants
Vs
Ali Hossain (Md) & ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hussain, C.J.: This appeal by special leave raises the question whether the Small Cause Court could declare a decree passed in a title suit by a civil Court a nullity, and whether the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction could reverse such a finding. If the first question is answered in the negative, then the second question will be in the affirmative. 

 2. Facts are, that the plaintiffs are appellants. The premises in suit consisting of 3 huts belonged to Gurudas Singha who died leaving three sons Santi Benode, Jyoti Benode and Shakti Benode and a widow Snehalata Hemalata. Snehalata relinquished her interest by way of family arrangement in favour of her three sons. In the recent settlement operation the suit plot was recorded in the names of Shakti brothers. Shakti Benode and his two brothers while in possession entered into a contract on 11.12.55 for sale of the suit premises in favour of proforma defendant 3 Nasiruddin and a Bainapatra was executed by the vendors in favour of one Mohammad Bakht, a benamdar of proforma-defendant 3. Shakti Benode and his two brothers did not execute the kabala, which led proforma-defendant 3 to bring Title Suit No. 38 of 1958 in the First Court of Subordinate' Judge, Sylhet, for specific performance of the said contract and obtain the decree and thereafter get a kabala executed and registered through court. He obtained delivery of possession through court on 8.5.66 in presence of the defendants. Proforma-defendant 3 made a gift of the suit premises by a registered deed of gift on 9.4.70, in favour of the plaintiffs. Proforma-defendant 3 after acquisition of title asked the defendants 1 and 2, who were residing there as tenants, to vacate the premises as he needed the house for building and rebuilding, and also asked them to pay rent at the rate of Taka 17.50 paisa per month for the two huts during the period of their stay. Defendant 1 Sudhangshu Kumar Chowdhury and defendant 2 Ramendra Narayan Chowdhury continued to reside on the suit land on various pleas. In the meanwhile, in 1966 the suit premises was about to be taken over by the Custodian of Enemy Property and proforma-defendant 3 moved the authority concerned for release of the same and get the property released by an order dated 18.8.66. Defendants 1 and 2 on getting scent of aforesaid order of release of the suit promises, instituted Tide Suit No. 199 of 1966 in the Court of Munsif, Sunamganj against the Custodian of Enemy Property and others on the allegations that they have taken settlement of the disputed premises from Shakti Benode on behalf of three brothers and their mother Snehalata, and got an ex pane decree of permanent injunction. Proforma-defendant 3 was not impleaded in the said suit. The defendants 1 and 2 secretly deposited rent in 1966 at the rate of Taka17.50 paisa in respect of the suit premises in the court of House Rent Controller in the name of Custodian, Enemy Property and Shakti Benode and others and thereafter stopped payment of rent to court also. The plaintiffs served quit notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on defendants 1 and 2, asking them to vacate the suit premises. In spite of such notice the defendants did not vacate. Thereupon, the plaintiffs filed the ejectment suit against them. 

 3. Defendants 1 and 2 contested the suit, contending that the suit premises belonged to Gurudas Singha. On his death the suit property devolved upon his widow Snehalata and his three sons. Plaintiff 4 Akmal Hossain's father pro-defendant 3 Nasiruddin Ahmed, created some false and collusive decree in Title Suit No. 38 of 1958, which they challenged as fraudulent and void. The plaintiffs acquired no interest by alleged gift from pro-defendant 3 and the interest of the original owners, namely, the heirs of Gurudas Singha remained unaffected. They denied to be tenants under plaintiffs and claimed tenancy under the original landlords. They contend that the rent was Taka 15.00 and Taka 10.00, total being Taka 25.00 per month. They denied the default or the bonafide requirement of the plaintiffs and challenged the relationship of landlord and tenant. They asserted the deposit of rent with Rent-Controller. Several issues were framed and the important one being the relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiffs and principal defendants 1 and 2. The trial Court on the question of jurisdiction and the value of the suit found that, the defence case that the rate of Taka 25.00 was not correct, but the plaintiffs case that the rate of rent at Taka 17.50 paisa was proved, and that the defendant after depositing the rent at the rate of Taka 17.50 paisa was estopped from saying that the rent of the suit premises still remained at Taka 25.00 and was of the view that had not the defendants any regard to the altered situation, then it was not understood as to why they deposited an amount which turned out to be the exact total rent of 14 (fourteen) months at the rate of Taka 17.50 paisa. He also found notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was valid. He, however, on the question of relationship of landlord and tenant went into the question of paramount title and found that the decree obtained by the predecessor of plaintiffs in specific performance of contract case was vitiated by fraud, and so held that the plaintiffs acquired no title by virtue of the gift, on the basis of which his title accrued. He therefore dismissed the suit. In revision, the learned Single Judge held that the trial Court which was a Small Cause Court had no jurisdiction to decide the question of title and that the finding on the question of fraud was also not based on proper reasoning and that there was a clear devolution of title in favour of the plaintiffs, and in that view of the matter he reversed that finding of the trial Court and decreed the suit. 

 4. Mr. Pal, the learned Counsel, appearing for the Appellants has contended with reference to section 23 of the Small Cause Court Act that the question of title cannot be gone into, but such question can be enquired incidentally. He, however, says, when the defendants raised the question of title, the plaint ought to have been returned for filing in a proper Court. As a proposition of law, the submission of Mr. Pal is sound, but from the findings of the two Courts below, we find it difficult to accept the challenge to the soundness of the learned Judge's decision. As has been observed that if the first question of the leave order does not stand, the second question automatically prevails. For setting aside the finding of the trial Court, Mr. Pal cannot with any amount of confidence challenge that finding of the learned Single Judge that the SCC Judge had no jurisdiction to go into the question of paramount title, and in so doing, to set side the decree of a civil Court obtained by the predecessor of the plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of contract. We find no error in the finding of the learned Judge. The Small Cause Court had no jurisdiction to go into the question of title, except incidentally, vide Ahmed Shah Khan Vs. Abdul Barkat 11 DLR 427. 

 5. There is a clear finding by the learned Judge that the plaintiffs stepped into the shoes of Santi Benode, Joyti Benode and Shakti Benode and that defendants 1 and 2 were inducted by Shand Benode as tenants and the plaintiffs having acquired valid title, stepped into the shoes of the landlords and have become landlord of defendants 1 and 2 in relation to the suit premises. What is wanting in the finding of the learned Judge is whether the defendants attorned to the plaintiffs on their acquisition of title. Though there is no clear finding by him in that respect, we find that the learned SCC Judge while disposing of the question of valuation of the suit, has in substance considered the question of relationship of landlord and tenant in the altered circumstances and his finding on that point has already been observed. The conclusion, arrived at by the SCC Judge that the story of fixation of Taka 17.50 paisa as the rent by the plaintiffs after they stepped into the shoes of Santi brothers by devolution of title, finds support from the deposit of the rent at that rate by the respondents. It appears that it has been asserted both in the plaint and in the evidence that the plaintiffs requested the defendants to pay rent, which they promised to pay but did not act upon the promise. This was denied by the defendants both in the written statement and in evidence. In the background of these pleadings and the evidence, the SCC Judge found that the rate of Taka 17.50 paisa as rent per month completely fits in with the case of the plaintiffs, and had not the defendants accepted the altered situation then it is not understood how the amount deposited by them turned to be total rent of 14(fourteen) months, at the rate of Taka 17.50 paisa, on the basis of which the defendants have deposited rent with the House Rent Controller. This finding, therefore, in substance has established that the plaintiffs have succeeded in proving the relationship of landlord and tenant. He, however, proceeded to examine the basis of paramount title of the plaintiffs, which the learned Judge has rightly reversed. There is enough materials on record to hold that the relationship of landlord and tenant was established by the plaintiffs. The other findings of service of quit notice and default have clearly been held in favour of the plaintiffs by the trial Court and so the learned Single Judge was justified in decreeing the suit.
